title: Intraday/overnight seasonality in Bitcoin (hour-of-day windows)
economic_hypothesis: Crypto trading activity is concentrated in particular clock windows (US cash hours, Asian open, overnight). If some windows persistently carry positive drift, a strategy that holds BTC only in those windows should earn it.
entry_rules: PARTIAL: hold BTC during a named hour window (the source highlights 22:00 and 23:00 UTC, and calls 04:00 the worst). The window itself is a mined parameter.
exit_rules: PARTIAL: exit at the end of the window (implied by the construction).
risk_rules: UNKNOWN as a source rule; a window strategy earns nothing when the drift is absent and still pays two round trips per day.
parameters: A single hour selection plus day-of-week conditioning.
claimed_metrics: companion backtest reports about 0.07% average return for the best hour; the source ranks 22:00/23:00 as best and 04:00 as worst
transaction_cost_model: NONE (the blog reproduction does not state fee assumptions)
external_results: Strategy-blog reproduction of an academic observation; no peer-reviewed tradability result in the registry for this line.
counter_evidence: About 7 bps gross for the best hour cannot pay a 23.791 bps round trip; entering and exiting daily is a guaranteed cost with the same magnitude as the effect.
Twenty-four hours x seven days is 168 candidate windows: selecting the best one is textbook multiple testing, and the source shows the ranking, not its stability.
Seasonality of this kind is exactly the 'different threshold' pattern the reentry policy rejects.
The project already has a strong internal result in the neighbouring space: intraday/daily price-directional effects are weak and cost-sensitive (WHERE_WE_ARE.md).
ambiguities: Whether the selected hour is stable out of sample is not shown.
No cost model, no turnover accounting.
replication_difficulty: TRIVIAL to run, which is the problem: it is a mining exercise, not a replication.
selection_note: Registered because a reader will meet this idea constantly online; rejected on the policy's own grounds (mined threshold) and on arithmetic (gross effect below the cost floor).
